propagation-001.question: Which is correct about how the ground wave used in medium-wave (MF) broadcasting propagates?
choices: Vertical polarization is used, and the wave reaches farther over the sea, where the ground conductivity is high, than over dry land
Horizontal polarization suffers less attenuation from the ground, so transmitting antennas are usually strung horizontally
The higher the frequency, the smaller the ground-wave attenuation, so shortwave travels farther by ground wave
propagation-001.explanation: The ground wave travels along the surface of the earth, driving current in the ground as it goes, so its attenuation is set by the conductivity and permittivity of the ground. Over seawater, with its high conductivity, the loss is small and the wave reaches much farther than over dry sand or rocky land. The electric field of a horizontally polarized wave is nearly short-circuited at the surface of the ground, which acts almost like a conductor, so vertical polarization is used for the ground wave, and medium-wave broadcasting uses antennas (towers) standing vertically on the ground. Ground-wave attenuation grows with frequency, so at shortwave the ground wave reaches only short distances, and long distances use reflection from the ionosphere.

propagation-002.question: Which is correct about the reflection of a radio wave incident on real ground (with finite conductivity) at a shallow angle (grazing the ground)?
choices: At grazing incidence the wave is almost entirely absorbed by the ground, so the reflected wave is weak and its interference with the direct wave can be ignored
The reflection coefficient for horizontal polarization has a Brewster angle at which reflection is almost zero, while vertical polarization has none
Regardless of polarization, as incidence approaches grazing the reflection coefficient approaches −1, and the reflected wave is nearly in antiphase with the direct wave
propagation-002.explanation: For reflection from flat ground, as the angle of incidence (the elevation angle from the ground) approaches 0, the reflection coefficient approaches a magnitude of nearly 1 and a phase of 180°, that is, −1, regardless of polarization. This is why the direct and reflected waves cancel in the far region of the two-ray model (over a perfectly conducting ground, the vertical-polarization coefficient would instead be +1). At grazing incidence the reflection actually becomes stronger, so the reflected wave cannot be ignored. It is vertical polarization that has an angle (the pseudo-Brewster angle) at which the magnitude of the reflection coefficient drops markedly; the magnitude of the horizontal-polarization reflection coefficient decreases only gradually as the angle increases, has no such minimum, and is nearly −1 at grazing incidence.

propagation-003.question: On a link over flat ground, the transmitting antenna height is 50 m, the distance is 5 km and the frequency is 3 GHz (wavelength 0.1 m). When the receiving antenna height is varied, the received field strength alternates between strong and weak because of interference between the direct and reflected waves. Which is closest to the height interval between the points of reinforcement? The path difference between the direct and reflected waves can be approximated by 2hthr/d (ht and hr are the transmitting and receiving antenna heights, d is the distance).
choices: 5 m
propagation-003.explanation: The path difference Δ = 2hthr/d is proportional to the receiving antenna height hr, so each time Δ changes by one wavelength the phase relationship of the two waves goes through a full cycle and a point of reinforcement appears again. The interval is Δhr = λd/(2ht) = 0.1 × 5000/(2 × 50) = 5 m. This variation of field strength with height is called a height pattern, and on line-of-sight links the receiving antenna height is chosen to sit on a point of reinforcement. 10 m is the value with the 2 dropped from the formula. 2.5 m is the mistake of thinking that reinforcement recurs every time the path difference changes by half a wavelength; what appears every half wavelength is the spacing between alternating points of reinforcement and cancellation.

propagation-004.question: Why is an "effective earth radius", 4/3 times the actual radius of the earth, used in the design of line-of-sight links?
choices: To include in the line-of-sight distance, by enlarging the earth, the radio waves that are reflected by the ionosphere and reach beyond the line of sight
To correct, by enlarging the earth, for the upward bending of radio waves, because the refractive index of the atmosphere increases with height
Because the refractive index of the atmosphere decreases slightly with height, the wave bends toward the ground; this is represented by a straight wave over a larger earth
propagation-004.explanation: In a standard atmosphere, the refractive index decreases slightly with height (the change in refractive index is about −40×10⁻⁶ per km), and the path of a radio wave bends downward, that is, slightly toward the ground. The bending of the wave and the curvature of the earth are relative, so instead of drawing the wave as straight, making the earth's radius k times larger (about 4/3 in a standard atmosphere) gives the same line-of-sight relationships. Thinking that the refractive index increases with height is the reverse; in that case the wave bends upward and k becomes less than 1. Ionospheric reflection is a phenomenon of low frequencies such as the HF band and has nothing to do with this correction.

propagation-005.question: Take the effective earth radius factor as k = 4/3 and the earth's radius as 6370 km. With a transmitting antenna height of 100 m and a receiving antenna height of 25 m, which is closest to the radio line-of-sight distance? The distance from an antenna at height h to the horizon is √(2kRh).
choices: About 62 km
About 54 km
About 46 km
propagation-005.explanation: The effective earth radius is kR = 4/3 × 6370 km ≈ 8493 km. The transmitting side gives √(2 × 8.493×10⁶ m × 100 m) ≈ 41.2 km and the receiving side √(2 × 8.493×10⁶ m × 25 m) ≈ 20.6 km, so the line-of-sight distance is their sum, about 62 km (61.8 km). The practical formula d ≈ 4.12(√h1 + √h2) km (heights in m) also gives 4.12 × (10 + 5) ≈ 61.8 km. About 54 km is the value with k = 1, ignoring atmospheric refraction. About 46 km is the mistake of calculating once with the sum of the two heights, 125 m; the distances to the horizon must be found separately for the transmitting and receiving sides and then added.

propagation-006.question: In the design of a line-of-sight microwave link, why are weather conditions in which the effective earth radius factor k becomes smaller than the standard 4/3 (for example 2/3) also examined?
choices: Because a small k makes radio waves bend strongly toward the ground, extending the line-of-sight distance and increasing interference from distant stations
Because the earth's bulge appears larger, so the Fresnel zone clearance around the middle of the path shrinks and diffraction loss may increase
Because a small k makes ionospheric reflection more likely, so microwaves reach distant stations beyond the line of sight and cause interference
propagation-006.explanation: The earth's bulge at a point along the path is d1d2/(2kR) (d1 and d2 are the distances from the two ends), and it grows as k becomes smaller. For example, at the center of a 50 km path it is about 37 m for k = 4/3 and about 74 m for k = 2/3, so the clearance between the line of sight and the ground or obstacles shrinks, and diffraction loss occurs when the first Fresnel zone is obstructed. In link design, the antenna heights are therefore chosen so that the needed clearance remains even under conditions where k is small. Line-of-sight distance extends and interference increases when k becomes large (conditions close to ducting). Microwaves pass through the ionosphere, so the value of k never causes ionospheric reflection.

propagation-007.question: Which is the correct condition for a "radio duct" to form in the troposphere, in which radio waves are trapped between the ground and an atmospheric layer and reach far beyond the line of sight? The change in refractive index is expressed in N units (N = (n − 1)×10⁶), and dN/dh is the change per km of height.
choices: When there is a layer in which dN/dh is less than −157 N/km (the refractive index decreases steeply with height)
When there is a layer in which dN/dh is positive (the refractive index increases with height), so the wave bends strongly toward the ground
In a standard atmosphere with dN/dh of about −40 N/km, where the curvature of the ray equals the curvature of the earth
propagation-007.explanation: The curvature of a radio wave's path is set by −dn/dh, and when dN/dh = −157 N/km the curvature of the wave equals the curvature of the earth (1/6370 km ≈ 157×10⁻⁶ /km). If the refractive index decreases more steeply than this, the wave bends toward the ground more strongly than the earth curves and is trapped, as if repeatedly reflected between the ground and the layer. In terms of the modified refractivity M = N + 157h, it is a layer with dM/dh < 0. It occurs with temperature inversions over the sea or dry air aloft, and causes unusual interference from distant stations. In a layer with positive dN/dh the wave bends upward (k < 1) and the line of sight actually becomes shorter. −40 N/km is the value for a standard atmosphere with k ≈ 4/3.

propagation-008.question: Midway between points with d1 = d2 = 4 km, there is a knife-edge obstacle projecting 10 m above the line of sight. The frequency is 3 GHz (wavelength 0.1 m). Using the diffraction parameter v = h√(2(d1 + d2)/(λd1d2)) and the approximate diffraction loss J(v) ≈ 6.9 + 20 log₁₀(√((v − 0.1)² + 1) + v − 0.1) dB, which is closest to the diffraction loss?
choices: About 6 dB
About 14 dB
About 43 dB
propagation-008.explanation: v = 10 × √(2 × 8000/(0.1 × 4000 × 4000)) = 10 × √0.01 = 1.0. J(1.0) = 6.9 + 20 log₁₀(√(0.81 + 1) + 0.9) = 6.9 + 20 log₁₀(2.245) ≈ 6.9 + 7.0 ≈ 13.9 dB, about 14 dB. Here the radius of the first Fresnel zone is √(0.1 × 4000 × 4000/8000) ≈ 14.1 m, so the obstacle projects about 0.7 times that above the line of sight. About 6 dB is the value for v = 0, when the tip just touches the line of sight. About 43 dB is the unit mistake of entering d1 and d2 in km while λ stays in m, which gives v ≈ 31.6.

propagation-009.question: Regarding the critical frequency of the ionosphere (the highest frequency at which a wave launched straight up is reflected back), which correctly describes the change when the maximum electron density of the layer becomes 4 times larger?
choices: It becomes 4 times larger (proportional to the electron density)
It does not change (the critical frequency is determined only by the height of the layer)
It becomes 2 times larger (proportional to the square root of the electron density)
propagation-009.explanation: Electrons in the ionosphere reflect radio waves below the plasma frequency fp = √(Ne²/(4π²ε0m)) ≈ 9√N Hz (N is the electron density in m⁻³) and pass waves above it. For vertical incidence, the plasma frequency at the layer's maximum electron density is the critical frequency, so if the electron density becomes 4 times larger, the critical frequency becomes √4 = 2 times larger. For example, N = 1×10¹² m⁻³ gives about 9 MHz. The mistake of making it proportional to the electron density forgets the square root. The critical frequency is set by the electron density, not by the height of the layer, and the electron density varies with day and night, season and solar activity according to the strength of the sun's ultraviolet radiation.

propagation-010.question: At a certain time the critical frequency of the F layer is 7 MHz. What is the maximum usable frequency (MUF) on a path where the angle at which the wave is incident on the layer (measured from the layer's normal, that is, from straight up) is 60°? Use the secant law MUF = fc/cos θ and treat the layer as flat.
choices: 14 MHz
3.5 MHz
About 8.1 MHz
propagation-010.explanation: The secant law expresses that an obliquely incident wave is reflected up to a higher frequency than a vertically incident one. MUF = fc/cos θ = 7 MHz/cos 60° = 7/0.5 = 14 MHz. The farther the station to be reached, the larger the angle of incidence and the higher the MUF. 3.5 MHz is the mistake of multiplying by cos θ instead of dividing. About 8.1 MHz is the value from dividing by sin 60°, confusing an angle measured from the horizontal with one measured from straight up (60° from the horizontal is 30° from straight up). On real links, a frequency of about 85% of the MUF (the optimum working frequency) is a guideline, to allow for ionospheric fluctuations.

propagation-011.question: In daytime shortwave communication, what is the main reason that lower frequencies reach distant stations less well?
choices: The lower the frequency, the more it penetrates the dense F layer and fails to return to the ground
The lower the frequency, the longer the wavelength, and free-space path loss grows in proportion to the square of the wavelength
Absorption in the D layer, which forms in the daytime, is roughly inversely proportional to the square of the frequency, so it is larger at lower frequencies
propagation-011.explanation: The D layer is an ionospheric layer that forms only in the daytime at heights of about 60–90 km. Because the air density there is high, electrons shaken by the radio wave collide with neutral molecules and take energy from the wave as heat. This absorption is roughly inversely proportional to the square of the frequency, so in the daytime lower frequencies are weakened more and the lowest usable frequency (LUF) rises. At night the D layer disappears, and even the lower medium-wave and shortwave frequencies reach far. It is, conversely, waves above the MUF that penetrate the layer and do not return. With the same antenna gain, free-space path loss is smaller at lower frequencies, so it is not the cause.

propagation-012.question: On a terrestrial link at frequencies above 10 GHz, which is correct when the attenuation by rain of the same intensity is compared for horizontal and vertical polarization?
choices: Raindrops are spherical, so rain attenuation does not depend on polarization
Large raindrops become flattened horizontally as they fall, so horizontal polarization suffers more attenuation than vertical polarization
Large raindrops become elongated vertically as they fall, so vertical polarization suffers more attenuation than horizontal polarization
propagation-012.explanation: Large raindrops a few mm in diameter are squashed on the underside by air resistance as they fall and take a horizontally flattened shape. The horizontal electric field therefore interacts more strongly with the drops, and at the same rain rate the specific attenuation (attenuation per km) for horizontal polarization is larger than for vertical polarization. Since there is a difference with polarization, treating raindrops as spherical is only an approximation. Thinking they are elongated vertically is the mistake of imagining raindrops as teardrop-shaped. Because the drop shape produces attenuation and phase shifts that differ with polarization, cross-polarization discrimination (XPD) also degrades in heavy rain, causing interference on links that use two polarizations.

propagation-013.question: On a terrestrial link at about 20 GHz, the specific attenuation at a certain rain rate is 2.5 dB/km, the path length is 8 km, and the distance reduction factor, which represents heavy rain falling on only part of the path, is 0.6. What is the estimate of the rain attenuation?
choices: 12 dB
20 dB
About 33 dB
propagation-013.explanation: Rain attenuation is found by multiplying the specific attenuation γ by the effective path length Leff = r × L. Leff = 0.6 × 8 km = 4.8 km, and A = 2.5 dB/km × 4.8 km = 12 dB. Heavy rain is concentrated in rain areas (rain cells) a few km across, so the longer the path, the smaller the fraction of it covered by rain of the same intensity, and the distance reduction factor is less than 1. 20 dB is the value obtained by forgetting the factor, as if rain of the same intensity fell over the whole path, and about 33 dB is the mistake of dividing by the factor. The specific attenuation is expressed in the form γ = kR^α (R is the rain rate in mm/h), with k and α set by frequency and polarization.

propagation-014.question: In the Hata formula for urban path loss, L = 69.55 + 26.16 log₁₀ f − 13.82 log₁₀ hb − a(hm) + (44.9 − 6.55 log₁₀ hb) log₁₀ d [dB] (f in MHz, hb the base station antenna height in m, d in km), with hb = 100 m, by how much does the path loss increase when the distance goes from 1 km to 10 km (other conditions unchanged)?
choices: 20 dB
propagation-014.explanation: The only term that depends on distance is (44.9 − 6.55 log₁₀ hb) log₁₀ d, so when the distance increases tenfold the loss increases by 44.9 − 6.55 × log₁₀ 100 = 44.9 − 13.1 = 31.8 dB. This corresponds to a path loss exponent of about 3.2, expressing faster attenuation than in free space (20 dB per tenfold distance, exponent 2) because of obstruction and scattering by buildings. 20 dB is the mistake of applying the free-space relationship. 44.9 dB is the value with the base station height term dropped; the higher the base station antenna, the more gently the loss grows with distance. a(hm) is the correction for the mobile antenna height and does not depend on distance, so it does not affect the difference.

propagation-015.question: Which is correct about empirical propagation models based on measurement data, such as the Okumura–Hata model?
choices: They are deterministic calculations that take into account the position and shape of each building, so they predict the received level at each location to within a few dB
Being fitted to measurements, they can have large errors outside their validity range of frequency, distance and antenna height; what they predict is the median received level
They are free-space path loss plus a constant independent of frequency, so they can be used in the same form at any frequency without regard to a validity range
propagation-015.explanation: The Okumura model summarizes in graphs a large number of measurements made around Tokyo, and the Hata formula turns them into easy-to-calculate formulas. The range of validity of the Hata formula is taken to be roughly frequencies of 150–1500 MHz, distances of 1–20 km and base station antenna heights of 30–200 m, and extended formulas such as COST-231 are used for higher frequencies. If they are extrapolated outside that range, the form of the formula no longer represents the physics, and the error can become large. What they predict is the median, and the location-to-location variation is handled separately as shadowing. Considering buildings one by one is what deterministic methods such as ray tracing do. The formula contains frequency terms (such as 26.16 log₁₀ f), so it is not just a constant added on.
